title: It’s Good to Talk
hook: A phone company that asked people to stay on the line.
before: People thought phone calls were expensive, so they kept them short. BT wanted to change that perception and get people talking for longer.
idea: Abbott Mead Vickers BBDO cast Bob Hoskins in three TV campaigns across 1994 and 1995, all built on one line: it’s good to talk.
shift: BT sold the conversation and let the minutes follow. The paper itself calls the campaign ‘a piece of social engineering’.
measure: Payback calculated with the Central ITV region, which did not see the campaign, as the control
evidence: Call duration rose in step with the campaign, and the Central region showed what happened without it. Very few national campaigns are tested this way. The public summary doesn’t say whether the £297m is revenue or profit.
lesson: If you want proof, hold something back. One region without the ads tells you more than a year of tracking.
test: BT kept the campaign off air in the Central ITV region. Comparing calls there with the rest of the country isolated what the advertising added.
links: View the BT materials in the Telephonic Youth exhibition
memorable: Casting Hoskins gave the campaign a familiar, down-to-earth voice. The line is short enough to say back in conversation, which suits a campaign about conversation.

creative.label: Watch BT’s Private Payphone (1994), from Telephonic Youth

take: Leaving a whole ITV region dark takes nerve, and it’s why this paper won the Grand Prix. Most brands still won’t give up the reach to learn the answer.
credit: IPA 1996 · Grand Prix · Abbott Mead Vickers BBDO for British Telecom

image.alt: Bob Hoskins looking over his shoulder in a dark cinema
image.credit: BT, Private Payphone (1994) · Telephonic Youth exhibition

title: Have a Break, Have a KitKat
hook: A chocolate bar that claimed the tea break.
before: Rowntree’s launched the bar in 1935 as Chocolate Crisp, after a worker suggested something a man could take to work in his pack. Early ads called it ‘the biggest little meal’ and ‘the perfect companion to a cup of tea’.
idea: In 1957 Donald Gilles at JWT London wrote ‘Have a break, have a KitKat’. It reached television in 1958 and tied the bar to a moment people already had every day.
shift: KitKat stopped selling a snack and started owning the pause. Later work stretched the break into new products, defended it when culture turned against breaks and rebuilt it for a distracted digital world.
measure: Estimated profit returned on each £1 invested in ‘Have a Break’, from 1958 to today
evidence: The 2026 paper estimates £3.56bn of incremental revenue and £677m of lifetime net profit from the idea. Any estimate that reaches back to 1958 has to fill gaps in the early data, and the public summary doesn’t explain how. It was entered by the brand’s current agencies and won a Commendation.
lesson: Name a moment people already have, and every later campaign has somewhere to live.
test: The paper values the idea across almost seventy years of activity and gives the result three ways: incremental revenue, lifetime net profit and profit per £1.
memorable: The line is an instruction. Six words tell you what to do and give you permission to do it, which worked in a 1958 canteen and still works on a phone screen.

creative.label: Watch the 1955–59 Rowntree’s adverts at the Yorkshire Film Archive

metric_label: Profit per £1 over the line’s life
take: Most brand lines last a few years. This one is older than colour television in Britain, and it now has a profit figure attached.
credit: IPA 2026 · Commendation · VML and OpenMind UK for Nestlé

image.alt: Vintage Rowntree’s advert showing a snapped KitKat and the Have a Break line
image.credit: Rowntree’s print advert · KitKat’s brand history

title: The Andrex Puppy
hook: A Labrador, a trailing roll and twenty years of leadership.
before: Toilet tissue was at risk of becoming a commodity. Andrex needed to show softness, strength and length without dwelling on what the product is for.
idea: The first plan was a little girl running through the house trailing a roll. Television regulators thought it would encourage children to be wasteful, so in 1972 a Labrador puppy took her place.
shift: The puppy carried every claim at once. A soft animal stood for softness, and an unbroken trail through the house showed strength and length.
measure: Andrex’s share of the market after twenty years of the puppy, per the 1992 IPA paper
evidence: Twenty years of share growth, plus Millward Brown blind testing that showed unusual loyalty. The paper argues the advertising held off Kleenex Velvet and helped sales, and it won the IPA’s ‘longer and broader effects’ category. The public summary gives no modelled return, so it sits a rung below most of this edition.
lesson: When the subject is awkward, find a stand-in that carries the claim and is a pleasure to watch.
test: The authors set two decades of share data against a well-funded rival launch, Kleenex Velvet, and added blind product tests on loyalty.
links: Watch a 1974 puppy film on J. Walter Thompson’s channel
memorable: The regulators’ objection created the brand’s best asset. A child making that mess looks naughty. A puppy making the same mess is irresistible.

creative.label: Watch the 1970s Softer Stronger Longer advert at the History of Advertising Trust

take: The regulator who blocked the little girl did Andrex a huge favour. Constraints often push you to the better idea.
credit: IPA 1992 · First Prize · J. Walter Thompson for Scott

image.alt: A Labrador puppy pulling a trail of toilet tissue through a doorway
image.credit: Andrex and J. Walter Thompson, Softer Stronger Longer (1970s) · History of Advertising Trust

title: The Rumour from Australia
hook: A launch that couldn’t mention butter.
before: Van den Berghs had the first margarine in the UK that looked and tasted like butter. The Margarine Regulations banned any comparison with butter, and shoppers distrusted butter-parity claims after Stork.
idea: Davidson Pearce and the broadcaster René Cutforth made no claim for Krona at all. The films talked about a brand that was a success in Australia, and the rumour there that it wasn’t margarine. Krona, they said, was its counterpart.
shift: A rule that should have silenced the product became the story. Krona took its sales mainly from butter, which was exactly the point.
measure: First prize in the first IPA Effectiveness Awards, 1980. A milestone, not a result
evidence: The 1980 paper used distribution, brand share, awareness, trial and repurchase data, with Taylor Nelson surveys and qualitative research. The public summary quotes none of the numbers. As the first winner it shows where the standard of proof started.
lesson: When the rules stop you making a claim, build the idea around the conclusion people will reach for themselves.
test: Krona launched at the end of 1978 in just two ITV regions, Harlech and Westward, with TV in short bursts. Two regions gave clean share and source-of-sales data to judge it by.
memorable: The whole launch rests on an implication. The viewer makes the comparison the advertiser wasn’t allowed to make.

creative.label: Watch the 1980 Krona advert at TVARK

take: The first IPA winner had no modelled return, just share data and surveys. Most of this page shows how far that bar has risen since 1980.
method: Regional launch, share data and surveys
credit: IPA 1980 · First Prize · Davidson Pearce for Van den Berghs

image.alt: A man talks to the camera from the front seat of a car

title: Drink Drive, 1979 to 2009
hook: Thirty years of making one more drink look like a terrible decision.
before: Britain had a legal limit and the breathalyser from 1967, yet drink-driving was still a common cause of death and serious injury on the roads.
idea: Successive governments ran one long campaign in four phases, aimed in turn at attitudes, acceptability, denial and the decision on the night. From 1987 to 1997 ‘Drinking and driving wrecks lives’ moved the focus from the offender to victims and their families.
shift: The argument changed as the drinker changed. The campaign worked first on what people thought about drink-driving, then on whether friends would accept it, then on the excuses drivers made, and finally on the choice itself.
measure: Lives the paper estimates the campaigns saved, with more than 10,000 serious injuries prevented
evidence: A modelled estimate of lives and injuries saved, valued at £3bn to society. The return varies widely by phase: £154, £12 and £38 for every £1 in the second, third and fourth. Enforcement, safer cars and drinking habits all changed over the same thirty years, so the model has to separate the campaign from them.
lesson: A long campaign can change its target as the problem changes. The drinker of 1979 needed a different argument from the drinker of 2009.
test: The authors modelled drink-drive casualties from 1979 to 2009, estimated how many were avoided because of the communications and put a value on the deaths and injuries prevented.
memorable: ‘Pudding’, from 1993, cuts from a family bringing in a blazing Christmas pudding to a phone call from the police. The end line becomes ‘Drinking and driving wrecks Christmas’.

creative.label: Watch 50 years of drink-drive films on the THINK! channel

take: This is the case I’d show anyone who says advertising can’t be measured. It counts lives, and it shows the return rising and falling as the strategy changed.
credit: IPA 2012 · Gold · Leo Burnett for the Department for Transport

image.alt: A barman looks straight at the camera in a dimly lit pub
image.credit: THINK! road safety, 50 Years of Drink Drive Campaigns · official YouTube thumbnail

title: Reassuringly Expensive
hook: A lager that sold its price as the proof.
before: In blind tests drinkers did not prefer Stella Artois to other draught lagers, and it was not stronger than several of them. What it did have was a higher price.
idea: Lowe Howard-Spink added one end-line to its press ads: ‘Reassuringly expensive’. The price stopped being a reason to hesitate and became the evidence of quality.
shift: Each group of drinkers read the line its own way. Connoisseurs heard flavour, ‘headbangers’ heard strength and style-seekers heard exclusivity. Keeping it in the press let each group hold its reading in private.
measure: Estimated return on advertising investment for the 1980s press campaign, with at least £7m of profit for Whitbread
evidence: The 1992 paper rules out sales force activity, packaging, sponsorship, promotions, strength and taste, then estimates at least £7m of profit and a 192% return. A later IPA paper models £242.76m of revenue from £21.1m of media and production between 1995 and 1999. The two papers cover different periods with different methods.
lesson: If a fact about your product puts people off, test whether it can become the proof.
test: The authors worked through the other explanations and discounted each one, then showed five years of sales growth rising with advertising weight. Growth stalled when rivals outspent Stella in the late 1980s, which supports the link.
links: Read the 1995 to 1999 profit paper · IPA
memorable: Brands usually explain a high price away. This one put it in the headline and let drinkers feel clever for paying it.

creative.label: Watch Balcony (1985–86) at the History of Advertising Trust

take: The blind-test detail is the whole case. Take the name away and nobody prefers it. Put the price back and they pay more. That gap is what a brand is worth.

image.alt: Stella Artois print advert with rows of beer glasses and the headline My shout, he whispered
image.credit: Stella Artois and Lowe Howard-Spink, My shout, he whispered · reproduced by WordDept

title: Love It or Hate It
hook: A spread that admitted half the country can’t stand it.
before: The market Marmite sold into was shrinking and many former buyers had drifted away. Its taste had always split opinion.
idea: In October 1996 the agency now called adam&eveDDB launched ‘Love it or hate it’. The ads gave the haters equal time and made the split itself the brand.
shift: Disliking Marmite became part of the appeal, and lapsed users came back. ‘The Marmite effect’ entered the language for anything that divides opinion.
measure: Incremental sales attributed to £12.4m of advertising by econometrics, 1995 to 2001
evidence: Econometrics credit £12.4m of advertising with £53.5m of extra sales, and estimate that without the advertising and PR sales would have fallen by 26%. In fact the brand grew about 5% a year in a declining market. The figures cover advertising and PR together.
lesson: Admitting a weakness everyone already knows can be more persuasive than denying it.
test: An econometric model estimated what sales would have done without the advertising and PR. The answer was a 26% fall over a period in which the brand actually grew.
memorable: Few brand lines become figures of speech. People call a film or a politician ‘Marmite’ without a thought of toast.

creative.label: Watch I Hate (1996–97) at the History of Advertising Trust

take: I’d have bet against a client approving an ad that gives equal time to people who hate the product. The model says it was one of the best decisions Marmite ever made.
credit: IPA 2002 · Silver · adam&eveDDB for Unilever Bestfoods

image.alt: A Marmite jar beside a hand spreading Marmite on toast
image.credit: Marmite and BMP DDB, I Hate (1996–97) · History of Advertising Trust

title: Should’ve Gone to Specsavers
hook: Two decades of jokes about not seeing properly.
before: Specsavers had advertised continuously since the 1980s, at high weight and with a broad appeal. In 2002 it found a line that could carry all that spend.
idea: Graham Daldry at The Agency, Specsavers’ in-house team, came up with ‘Should’ve gone to Specsavers’ in 2002. Each ad shows a small disaster caused by poor eyesight, like a farmer shearing his sheepdog.
shift: Poor eyesight became a running joke the whole country was in on. The line turned into something people say to each other after any blunder.
measure: Incremental profit attributed to nearly £500m of Specsavers advertising across thirty years
evidence: The paper credits nearly £500m of advertising with £1.1bn of incremental profit. That covers all Specsavers advertising since the 1980s, including the years before the line, and a thirty-year estimate blends many campaigns and market changes.
lesson: A line that frames the problem as a joke can be renewed for decades without wearing out.
test: The 2014 paper looks at thirty years together: continuous presence, a high share of voice, humour and consistent brand assets. It credits the system rather than any single ad.
memorable: Every execution follows the same shape: a mistake, a beat, then the line. You can predict the ending and still laugh.
take: I like that this came from an in-house team. The best line in British optics was written by people who knew the business inside out.
credit: IPA 2014 · Gold · Manning Gottlieb OMD for Specsavers

image.alt: Black-and-white thumbnail from Sheepdog showing a sheep and a sheepdog

title: Lamb on Australia Day
hook: A meat that wrote itself into a national holiday.
before: The weeks around Australia Day had traditionally been a slow time for lamb.
idea: Meat & Livestock Australia set out to make lamb the Australia Day meal. From 2005 the former footballer Sam Kekovich delivered a yearly mock-patriotic rant, starting with the claim that vegetarians were un-Australian for not eating lamb.
shift: By 2010 eating lamb on Australia Day had become a tradition. The case compares it to chocolate eggs at Easter.
measure: Return on marketing investment: A$122m from A$8.5m, per the IPA case
evidence: A ROMI of 14.22 to 1 across the programme, worth A$122m on A$8.5m of spend. The summary doesn’t say whether the return is revenue or profit, and it covers the whole ten-year programme, not only the Kekovich films.
lesson: Owning a date gives a campaign a deadline every year and a sales spike you can measure.
test: The case calculates the return across the full ten years of Australia Day activity, which lets the effect build year on year.
memorable: The first ad drew complaints from vegetarian groups, and the Advertising Standards Bureau let it run because it was plainly satire. The row became part of the fame.

creative.label: Watch the 2005 film on the LambAustraliaDay channel

metric_label: Return on marketing over ten years
take: Inventing a tradition sounds like a fantasy brief. It worked because the ads were funny enough that people wanted to join in.

image.alt: Sam Kekovich delivering his address in front of an Australian flag
image.credit: Meat & Livestock Australia and BMF, We Love Our Lamb (2005) · LambAustraliaDay on YouTube

title: The Long Wait
hook: A boy who can’t wait for Christmas, for the best reason.
before: In mid-2009 John Lewis was struggling in a hard economy, and its recent advertising had not worked.
idea: The agency adam&eve bet on emotional advertising, especially on TV, with Christmas as the centrepiece. In ‘The Long Wait’ a boy counts down the days, then on Christmas morning walks past his own presents to give his parents the one he wrapped.
shift: A department store’s Christmas ad became something the country looked forward to. More people visited, they came more often and they spent more.
measure: Incremental profit from the advertising that began in mid-2009, alongside £1,074m of incremental sales
evidence: £1,074m of incremental sales and £261m of incremental profit in just over two years. The figures cover all John Lewis advertising from mid-2009, not ‘The Long Wait’ alone. Because John Lewis is employee-owned, the extra profit also raised the bonus its partners share.
lesson: Make the ad people want to see, then follow it all the way to the till.
test: The case traces the chain from fame to footfall to spend, with more visitors coming more often and spending more, and converts it into incremental sales and profit.
memorable: The ending works because the boy’s impatience looks selfish for most of the film. The soundtrack is a hushed cover of The Smiths’ ‘Please, Please, Please, Let Me Get What I Want’.

creative.label: Watch ‘The Long Wait’ on John Lewis’s channel

metric_label: Incremental profit in just over two years
take: Everyone remembers the tears. Fewer people know the paper put a profit figure on them, and that the staff shared in it.
credit: IPA 2012 · Gold · adam&eveDDB and Manning Gottlieb OMD for John Lewis

image.alt: A boy alone on a swing in The Long Wait
image.credit: John Lewis, The Long Wait (2011) · official YouTube thumbnail

title: A Husband’s Thank-You
hook: A detergent repositioned as a gift from husband to wife.
before: P&G launched Tide Naturals in rural India in 2009. Shoppers seemed convinced by the product, but sales fell short of expectations.
idea: Research by P&G India and Leo Burnett found that husbands, rather than their wives, decided which detergent to buy. The campaign turned Tide Naturals from an item on a shopping list into a way for a husband to show his appreciation.
shift: The advertising spoke to the person who made the decision and gave him a reason to buy that went beyond cleaning.
measure: ROMI of 7 reported in the IPA case for 2012 to 2013
evidence: A reported ROMI of 7, with Tide Naturals described as the fastest-growing laundry brand in rural India. The summary doesn’t say whether the return is revenue or profit, or how it was modelled.
lesson: Find out who actually makes the decision. It is often not the person in your ads.
test: The insight came first, from research into who held the purchase decision. The return was then calculated for the 2012 to 2013 campaign.
memorable: It turns a chore into something worth noticing. The product becomes the sign that the husband sees the work.

creative.label: Watch a Haryanvi Tide Naturals advert on YouTube

take: Commercially sharp, and it put the real buyer in the picture. I’d still like to see it remade with the husband doing the washing.
credit: IPA 2014 · Leo Burnett India for Procter & Gamble

image.alt: A woman holding a green Tide Naturals packet beside her husband
image.credit: P&G and Leo Burnett India, Haryanvi Tide Naturals advert · YouTube upload cited by Hindustan Times

title: Do It for Denmark
hook: A travel firm that offered holidays as the cure for a falling birth rate.
before: Danes were booking budget airlines and travel websites themselves. Spies, a 60-year-old operator known for family package holidays to the Mediterranean, was losing its place.
idea: Robert/Boisen & Like-minded made a tongue-in-cheek film suggesting Danish couples should travel to have more sex and lift the country’s flagging birth rate. A year later ‘Do it for Mom’ turned the joke on would-be grandparents.
shift: A package-holiday brand earned a role in a national conversation about population, and sold more city breaks and activity holidays because of it.
measure: Estimated revenue for every euro across ‘Do it for Denmark’ and ‘Do it for Mom’, on a €670,000 budget
evidence: An estimated €5.80 of revenue for every euro across both campaigns. The summary’s net profit figure is incomplete, so only the revenue return is quoted here. Revenue is not profit, and the method isn’t described.
lesson: A small budget can still buy proof if the idea creates its own coverage.
test: The return is calculated on a small, known budget of €670,000 across both films, set against sales of Spies city breaks and activity holidays.
memorable: It presents a national statistic with a straight face and lets the absurdity do the work.

creative.label: Watch ‘Do It For Denmark!’ on Spies Rejser’s channel

take: Cheeky, cheap and measured. Proof isn’t only for brands with big budgets.
credit: IPA 2016 · Bronze · Robert/Boisen & Like-minded for Spies Travels

image.alt: A woman smiling in the doorway of a hotel room
image.credit: Spies Rejser, Do It For Denmark! (2014) · official YouTube thumbnail

title: The Red Moment
hook: A fruit that became a Chinese New Year gift.
before: Chile’s cherry growers were expanding production fast. Demand in China had to more than triple in four years, ahead of supply, to protect a premium price.
idea: The Chilean Fresh Fruit Exporters Association tied its cherries to Chinese New Year. Red stands for good fortune and joy, the price suggests wealth, and the campaigns invited people to share cherries at every ‘red moment’.
shift: A commodity became a seasonal treat with a meaning. Cherry eaters in China rose from 42 million in 2016/17 to 134 million by 2019/20.
measure: Estimated incremental export revenue generated by the strategy, 2016 to 2020
evidence: An estimated US$111.1m of incremental export revenue, while total export value rose from US$552m to US$1.4bn. Much of that rise came with a planned expansion in production, so the estimate matters more than the headline growth.
lesson: Tie the product to an occasion that already means something, and let the meaning do the persuading.
test: Four campaigns over four seasons, for trade buyers and shoppers, held one positioning. The case estimates the marketing’s share of growth that more supply was also driving.
memorable: It borrows a colour that already carries meaning in the market. The fruit didn’t change. What it said when you gave it did.

creative.label: Watch the ASOEX case film on the IPA’s Vimeo channel
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: This was the case I knew least about, and it’s one of the cleverest. A trade body found a cultural moment and built four years around it.
credit: IPA 2022 · Bronze · ASOEX for the Chilean Fresh Fruit Exporters Association

image.alt: A woman holding a bowl of cherries against red and white circles in a Cherries from Chile promotion
image.credit: Cherries from Chile, 2019–20 China campaign artwork · Produce Report

title: Anima Sarda
medium: TV, with projects on the island
hook: A Sardinian beer that proved its roots before selling them.
before: Ichnusa had been brewed in Sardinia for over a century and owned by Heineken since 1986, but until 2017 it was sold only on the island. A national launch risked making a local favourite look like a big brewer’s product.
idea: A black-and-white campaign, ‘Anima Sarda’ or Sardinian soul, challenged mainland stereotypes about Sardinians and the idea of the island as only a holiday spot. The brand backed it on the island with beach clean-ups, returnable bottles and a donated fire engine.
shift: Ichnusa went from Italy’s ninth-biggest beer brand to third in four years. Penetration tripled and its value share nearly quadrupled.
measure: Estimated profit returned for each euro invested in the communications strategy
evidence: An estimated €9.86 of profit for every euro invested. The national launch also had Heineken’s distribution behind it, which the estimate has to separate from the communications.
lesson: If you need to look authentic, do something for the place before you advertise it.
test: The paper estimates profit per euro across the national roll-out, and tracks awareness, penetration and value share as the brand moved from one island to the whole country.
memorable: The films are faces, gestures and landscapes in black and white, closer to a documentary than a beer ad.

creative.label: Watch ‘Anima Sarda’ on Birra Ichnusa’s channel

take: The fire engine is my favourite detail in this edition. It is hard to accuse a brand of faking its roots when it is helping the island fight fires.

image.alt: A black-and-white close-up of a face with Italian text from Anima Sarda
image.credit: Birra Ichnusa, Anima Sarda (2017) · official YouTube thumbnail

title: Für mehr O in deinem Leben
hook: A network that claimed the ‘Oh!’ you make at a great clip.
before: After years of losing customers, O2 had fallen from second to fourth in the German market.
idea: BBDO built 15-second ads from popular existing clips, rebranded as ‘O’ moments, then extended the idea to podcasts and clips from a hit German TV show. The insight was that content is only as good as the network it plays on.
shift: The brand name became the sound people make when something surprises them, and the network took the credit for the moment.
measure: ROMI reported in the IPA case, alongside 740,000 more new customers than Vodafone
evidence: A ROMI of 190%, 2% revenue growth and €50.2m of net profit, with 740,000 more new customers than Vodafone. The customer comparison describes the market. The ROMI is the estimate of what the advertising itself returned.
lesson: If your product is invisible, sell the moment it makes possible.
test: The case compares O2’s customer growth with Vodafone’s and estimates a return on the marketing spend, with profit attributed to the activity.
memorable: It turns the brand name into a reaction. Every ‘Oh!’ is a small brand mention the viewer makes without being asked.

creative.label: Watch a 2019 spot on the 48k music studio’s channel

take: Telecoms ads usually shout about coverage maps. Borrowing the internet’s best clips and claiming the reaction is a smarter way to say the same thing.
credit: IPA 2020 · BBDO Germany and Telefónica Germany

image.alt: Friends watching a phone, framed by an O2 signal indicator
image.credit: Telefónica Germany and BBDO, Für mehr O in deinem Leben (2019) · 48k studio upload
